svg.title: Build an event loop from basic pieces
svg.desc: Unified OS-independent teaching model for submitted calls, timers, and persistent bus watches. Caller and worker share a mutex, a source registry, and a counting semaphore for registration notifications. add_source appends under the mutex, then releases the semaphore. Each source provides is_ready(now_s), wait_s(now_s), signal, persistent, and dispatch(). The worker snapshots wake inputs under the mutex, removes a ready source only when it is not persistent, and dispatches after unlocking. Otherwise it blocks in wait_for_events on the snapshot of semaphore and external source notifications, or a timeout. This conceptual blocking helper consumes a semaphore permit for a wake input; bus readiness remains until consumed. Call dispatch invokes its stored callback once. BusWatch dispatch pops one message and supplies bus and msg to its handler while retaining the watch. Normal callback returns and ordinary asynchronous bus delivery are shown. The first example submits say_hello; the second submits a no-argument wrapper supplying Vincent as an argument. The third maps source-verified AM registration to the same source contract and dispatch model. Source methods and wait_for_events are pedagogical abstractions, not literal GLib APIs or a complete GLib implementation.
svg.text: Build an event loop from basic pieces
Generic pseudocode + AM mapping · one worker · submitted calls, timers, and persistent bus watches

g.text: TERM COLORS · each category keeps its color across code and prose

svg.text: One blocking helper waits for semaphore permits, bus activity, or a timeout: wait_for_events().

g.text: BUILD THE SHARED STATE AND DEFINE THE FUNCTIONS
Shared by the caller and the worker started in block 4.
The lock protects sources; the semaphore stores wakeup permits.
add_source() is shared by call and bus-watch registration.
Call stores callback + due_s and uses the contract below.
delay_s=0 is immediate; a positive delay schedules a timer.
Check under the lock; dispatch after unlocking; keep persistent watches.
# Notification or timeout: repeat the loop.
wait_inputs is a snapshot of wake + source notifications.
wait_for_events blocks on any input or timeout; it does not spin.
For the wake input, it consumes a semaphore permit with acquire().
ONE SHARED SOURCE CONTRACT · TWO IMPLEMENTATIONS
run_loop() uses the same fields and operations in both columns; wait_s() returns a duration in seconds and never blocks.
START IT, THEN FOLLOW ONE SUBMISSION
Illustrative normal path: let the worker reach its empty-source wait before the caller submits say_hello.
4 Create the thread, then start it
Run these lines on the main / caller thread.
Construction creates the thread object; start begins run_loop().
The worker blocks in wait_for_events() while no input is ready.
Define the example function, then submit it.
Passing say_hello does not call it on this caller thread.
6 submit() stores the source, then signals
Following step 2; illustrative state after the append:
The semaphore signals that the source registry changed.
7 Worker wakes and claims the ready source
if not source.persistent: # True for Call
The lock is released before dispatch().
8 Invoke the same function on this worker; return to the loop
The source was removed in step 7, so this submitted call runs once.
Callback returns → next loop iteration → no sources → wait_for_events().
Why a signal is not lost: release() adds a permit that wait_for_events() can consume even when signaled before the wait.
For the wake input it uses acquire(); bus readiness and timeouts can also end the wait.
SECOND EXAMPLE · CALLER PASSES A FUNCTION REFERENCE WITH ARGUMENTS
Separate example: say_hello now requires a name argument; a no-argument wrapper supplies it.
Caller: define and submit a no-argument wrapper
say_hello(name) requires a name; the wrapper requires none.
submit() stores the wrapper reference in the new source:
The wrapper's body runs later, on the worker thread.
Worker: invoke the wrapper with no arguments
run_loop() dispatches the Call source; its dispatch() invokes callback():
The submitted callable is the wrapper; that wrapper supplies the required argument when the worker invokes it.
Both examples use the same submit(), source storage, semaphore, and run_loop().
THIRD EXAMPLE · GSTREAMER BUS MESSAGES USE A PERSISTENT WATCH
AM setup for one configured monitoring pipeline; self is that pipeline's existing SxmGStreamer object.
The shared source contract and loop above already support this persistent bus source.
The bus watch supplies is_ready(), signal, persistent, wait_s(), and dispatch(); the same loop uses all five.
1 AM connects the handler to the bus
The same pipeline bus is used throughout this example.
2 Install the watch on the assigned worker
The watch attaches to its thread-default GLib context.
GStreamer-managed processing remains a black box.
The message lives in the bus queue.
The bus's readiness notification can wake the GLib worker.
One persistent source represents the bus watch.
4 Existing GLib worker delivers the message
BusWatch.dispatch() pops msg, then its adapter invokes AM:
Framework dispatch supplies bus + msg to the bound method.
The watch remains registered after the handler returns.
How the base model above handles this watch
BusWatch names the conceptual persistent source; the contracts below describe behavior, not GLib implementation code.
The same is_ready(now_s) call is used in block 3.
Call checks time; BusWatch checks pending messages.
The bus adapter supplies handler(bus, msg).
Wait only if no source is ready
Block 3 snapshots wake + bus notifications under the lock, then blocks outside it in wait_for_events().
One watch, many messages: the same source becomes ready again whenever another message is available.
submit() installs the watch once; each bus message uses the existing worker and watch, rather than creating another Call.
Unified teaching model · source operations and wait_for_events are conceptual · AM registration calls are source-verified
